title: How to Extract Large Volumes of SAP Pricing Data into SAP Datasphere Without Running Out of Memory
author: ArcherZhang
text:
If you have ever tried to pull sales pricing condition records from SAP S/4HANA into SAP Datasphere using a generic OData connection and hit a TSV_TNEW_PAGE_ALLOC_FAILED short dump, you are not alone. High-volume pricing tables are one of the most common sources of memory failures in OData-based extraction. This post documents a tested solution: pagination for the initial full load and filter-based delta extraction for ongoing refreshes. 
 The Problem 
 The S/4HANA OData service API_SLSPRICINGCONDITIONRECORD_SRV exposes sales pricing condition records across multiple entity sets. When the underlying tables hold millions of rows — which is typical in any production system with complex pricing — a single unbounded OData GET request forces the ABAP application server to allocate all result rows into memory at once. The runtime error TSV_TNEW_PAGE_ALLOC_FAILED is the ABAP kernel's way of saying it ran out of roll area before it could return the response. 

 The knock-on effect is that neither the initial load nor any subsequent refresh completes successfully, leaving the Datasphere local table empty or stale. 

 Solution Overview 
 The fix has two parts that address different phases of the data pipeline: 
 Pagination in Datasphere for the initial full load — prevents S/4 from building one giant result set in memory. 
 Filter-based delta extraction for daily refreshes — uses an S/4 OData feature to retrieve only records changed within a configurable time window. 
 Part 1: Initial Full Load with Pagination 
 Connection Settings 
 Create or reuse a generic OData connection in Datasphere pointing to the S/4 communication arrangement URL. Set the OData version to V2, which is what API_SLSPRICINGCONDITIONRECORD_SRV exposes. 
 Data Model 
 The pricing API splits condition records across entity sets by validity type (date-dependent, quantity-based, and so on). The recommended data model is a union of those validity entities, then joined to the main record entity. This mirrors the logical structure of the underlying ABAP condition tables and avoids cartesian joins. 

 Data Flow Configuration 

 Open the data flow and configure three areas: 
 Data Flow level: Dynamic Memory Allocation 
 Enable this setting. Pricing condition data is wide and joins amplify row width further. Without dynamic allocation, the Datasphere execution engine can exhaust its default memory ceiling before the run finishes. 
 Source node: Fetch Size and Batch Query 
 In the properties of the OData source node, enable Fetch Size and Batch Query. This activates server-side pagination. When the data flow starts, Datasphere first sends a $count request to learn the total row count, then issues sequential OData calls using $top and $skip to page through the result set in manageable chunks. Neither call ever asks S/4 to extract all rows simultaneously, which eliminates the memory pressure that triggered the short dump. 
 Example paging sequence emitted by Datasphere: 
 GET .../A_SlsPrcgConditionRecord/$count 
 GET .../A_SlsPrcgConditionRecord?$top=50000&$skip=0 
 GET .../A_SlsPrcgConditionRecord?$top=50000&$skip=50000 
 ... 
 Target node: Update Records By Primary Key (UPSERT) 

 Enable UPSERT on the target node. This makes reruns safe: if a run is interrupted and restarted, already-written records are updated rather than duplicated. It also makes the same flow reusable for delta loads. 
 Part 2: Delta Extraction for Daily Refreshes 
 The S/4HANA Feature: NumberOfDaysSinceCreation , NumberOfDaysSinceLastChange 
 API_SLSPRICINGCONDITIONRECORD_SRV exposes a virtual filter property called NumberOfDaysSinceCreation , NumberOfDaysSinceLastChange on the A_SlsPrcgConditionRecord entity. Setting it to 1 returns only records that were created or modified in the last calendar day, without any custom ABAP code on the S/4 side. 
 Delta OData request: 
 GET /sap/opu/odata/sap/API_SLSPRICINGCONDITIONRECORD_SRV/A_SlsPrcgConditionRecord?$filter=NumberOfDaysSinceLastChange eq 1 
 You can parameterise this value in the Datasphere data flow to control the lookback window. Set it to 2 or 3 on Mondays to catch weekend changes. 
 Delta Data Model 

 For the delta flow, union two sets of records: 
 Records filtered by creation date (new records). 
 Records filtered by last-change date (updated records). 
 Both branches expand to the validity entity. In the OData source node properties, set Depth to 2. This instructs Datasphere to issue $expand to the associated validity entity in the same OData call, avoiding a separate roundtrip. 
 The target is the same local table used by the full load. With UPSERT enabled, changed records overwrite existing rows and new records are inserted cleanly on every scheduled run. 
 Monitoring the Runs 
 After starting a data flow run, open the data flow in Data Builder and switch to the Monitoring view. Two tabs are available: 
 Messages: execution log entries, warnings, and error details. 
 Metrics: row counts processed per source and target node, memory consumed, and elapsed time per stage. 
 For the paginated initial load, watch the row counter in Metrics increment in batches. This confirms that $top/$skip cycling is working rather than a single unbounded fetch that would trigger the memory error again. 
 Summary 
 Four settings in Datasphere and one S/4 OData feature eliminate the memory crash and enable a sustainable incremental load pattern: 
 Dynamic Memory Allocation on the data flow: prevents Datasphere-side memory exhaustion on wide, joined result sets. 
 Fetch Size + Batch Query (pagination) on the OData source: breaks S/4 reads into bounded $top/$skip pages, preventing TSV_TNEW_PAGE_ALLOC_FAILED. 
 UPSERT on the target: makes reruns and delta merges idempotent. 
 NumberOfDaysSinceLastChange filter: offloads delta filtering to S/4 with zero custom code. 
 The same pattern applies to any high-volume OData entity in S/4HANA. If you are hitting memory errors on a different service, start with pagination and dynamic memory allocation. Those two settings alone resolve the majority of cases. 
 Remark 
 During the OData service execution in the S/4 backend, you may not only run out of memory, but also encounter processing timeouts, e.g. 10 mins. In this case, you may need to create an additional source entity with different filters in your data flow. Or even a different data flow.

title: SAP Build Process Automation – Use Principal Propagation (SCI/IAS) in Actions sample: CAP Services
author: ChingHong
text:
This post demonstrates how to connect SAP Build Process Automation (SBPA) to CAP (Node.js) API services using principal propagation. The same approach can also be applied when connecting SAP Integration Suite MCP to CAP (Node.js) API services. 
 There is an existing published blog SAP Build Process Automation – Use Principal Propa... - SAP Community, demonstrates principal propagation from SBPA (XSUAA) to CAP API Services (XSUAA) using OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion. 
 In contrast, this scenario is showing how SBPA (XSUAA) communicating with CAP API services secured by SAP Cloud Identity Services (SCI/IAS) through OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion under the same BAIP Subaccount. and reusing the same CAP Services built in the previous article, MCP Server with Integration Suite, expose CAP API ... - SAP Community. 
 Note: 
 OAuth2JWTBearer does not appear to support the authentication flow from SBPA (XSUAA) to CAP API services secured by SCI/IAS, even when both applications are deployed within the same SAP BAIP subaccount. 
 SCI is referring to SAP Cloud Identity Services → SAP Build Process Automation (Authenticated via XSUAA) 
 → BTP Destination Service (OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion) 
 → CAP Node.js API Services (executed as the authenticated user) 
 Pre-requisite: 
 SAP BTP with Cloud Foundry Enabled 
 SAP Build Process Automation 
 SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS) 
 1. CAP Services creation and deploy 
 This writing will reuse the CAP services created on the previous writing. Refer to the blog MCP Server with Integration Suite, expose CAP API ... - SAP Community step 1. 
 2. Establish Trust between BAIP/BTP destination with SAP SCI/IAS 
 Setup the Subaccount as Corporate Idp in the SAP Cloud Identity Services 
 Information: SAML Bearer Assertion Flow between Cloud Foundry Applications | SAP Help Portal 
 Navigate to BAIP → Destination Trust → Export the metadata.xml 

 Navigate to SAP Cloud Identity Services Admin Console → Identity Providers → Corporate Identity Providers 

 Upload the Subaccount SAML metadata.xml that downloaded in previous step, the rest of the fields will be auto populated. 

 Enable Identity Federation 

 3. Setup Provider App - CAP API Services authentication information 
 Ensure the Application has enabled the trust all corporate identity provider or restrict to only the corporate identity provider (subaccount) created in previous step 

 Always enable the principal propagation in this section. Note: even though this checkbox does not impact anything at this moment, but it is good to enable this in case SAP updated the authentication framework on checking this checkbox. 

 Ensure the SAML Bearer option is enabled. 

 Note: This can be either configured in MTA file or directly update in SCI, preferable configure this option in MTA file, as any future deployment will override any manual changes in SCI. 
 Create a new service key for SBPA and take note of the client id, client secret and url 

 4. Create BAIP/BTP Destination - OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion 
 Create a destination will be used by SBPA to consume the CAP Services 
 Property Value 
 Authentication OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion 
 Name <Any> 
 Token Service User <From Previous Step - client id> 
 Token Service Password <From Previous Step - client secret> 
 URL <Target CAP API Services URL> 
 AuthnContextClassRef urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:PreviousSession 
 Audience https://<ias tenant> 
 Client Key <From Previous Step - client id> 
 Name Id Format urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:emailAddress 
 User Id Source email 
 Additional Properties 
 sap.processautomation.enabled true 
 BuildApps.Enabled true 
 sap.applicationdevelopment.actions.enabled true 

 5. SBPA Setup and Testing 
 This demo will not show step by step on action and process creation. You can go through the learning from SAP Learning website. 
 SBPA Control tower -> Import the created destination 

 Create new Action - CAP Bookshop Service - Admin and test with the destination 
 Can refer to the step 4 on how to extract the API metadata - MCP Server with Integration Suite, expose CAP API ... - SAP Community 

 Create a Process, test create new Author via the API 

 Choose the desired destination during deployment 

 Launch the form, enter the information and click Submit 

 Check the monitoring to confirm the new Author is created with named-user. 

 6. Alternative option - create separate Cloud Identity Services instance with dependency setup 
 This approach enables a standalone SAP Cloud Identity Services (SCI/IAS) instance to act as the consumer of the CAP API services. Cloud Identity Service Instance A (with CAP application bound, without SAML Bearer Authentication enabled)
 |-- with Dependency setup Cloud Identity
Service Instance B (without CAP application bound, separate client ID B, with SAML Bearer Authentication enabled)
 |-- Destination setup with client ID B, target CAP API
SAP SBPA calls the CAP services via Destination OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion 
 Create a separate Cloud Identity Service instance in BAIP/BTP 
 Service: Cloud Identity Services 
 Plan: application 
 Instance Name: <any> 
 Create service key and take note of the client id, client secret and url

 },

}

 Application: <SCI instance application that have CAP bound>

 Goto BTP setup new destination

 Name <Any>

 Name Id Format urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:emailAddress

 BuildApps.Enabled true 
 sap.applicationdevelopment.actions.enabled true

title: The Next Leap in Public Services Starts Behind the Scenes
author: Andre Bechtold
text:
Artificial intelligence can do far more for public administration than answer questions or digitize individual interactions. 
 Unify every mission-critical function to drive government efficiency and innovation 

 Learn how 

 Its real potential emerges when AI connects with the data and processes behind public services, turning a citizen request into coordinated action across the administration. 

 For public institutions, there is another essential requirement: innovation must go hand in hand with transparency, accountability, and digital sovereignty. SAP combines decades of process expertise with enterprise applications, data, AI, and sovereign cloud technologies. 

 S.Public , the new SAP Experience Center location for the public sector, brings these capabilities to life. It officially opened in Berlin on October 12, 2026. 

 From a citizen request to coordinated action 

 Damage in a public space can be reported digitally in a matter of moments. But that is where the actual administrative process begins: determining responsibilities, planning the work, checking resources and budgets, procuring materials if needed, and closing the case. SAP solutions can connect citizen engagement, maintenance, procurement, and financial management across this end-to-end process. 

 At S.Public, a playground scenario makes this tangible. A citizen notices damage, such as a broken swing, and reports it by smartphone. The steps that follow show how a single report becomes coordinated action. The real innovation is not the reporting form itself, but the intelligently connected processes behind it. 

 When AI understands the administrative context 

 The same principle applies to public funding. Applications involve documents, eligibility requirements, and financial information. AI can check submitted materials for completeness and consistency, flag missing information early, and provide employees with an explained recommendation for further review. The final decision remains with the responsible public authority. 

 A funding application for a solar installation illustrates this approach in Berlin. The SAP capability behind it is broadly applicable: AI is embedded where employees evaluate information and manage processes. Rather than automating isolated tasks, it supports the broader administrative context. 

 When digital sovereignty meets AI 

 How can sensitive data be used with AI while remaining under an organization’s own control? SAP Sovereign Cloud addresses four dimensions of digital sovereignty: data, operational, technical, and legal sovereignty. 

 At S.Public, this concept becomes something visitors can actually walk through. The new Sovereign Cloud Showroom makes SAP’s security and sovereignty concept physically tangible for the first time. Visitors pass through three security zones: administration, control, and restricted zones. They experience firsthand how the operating environment for SAP Sovereign Cloud and the protection of classified information work together. 

 A public sector scenario at a seaport shows how this can be combined with intelligent analysis. SAP solutions and the AI assistant Joule bring together selected data from internal and external systems in a sovereign environment. Data on vessel arrivals, terminals, containers, and available inspection capacity is turned into a prioritized overview. Analysts can query it in natural language, while the responsible public officials decide which inspections to carry out. 

 More than a place for demonstrations 

 The three examples point to a common development: public services become more intelligent when applications, data, and AI work together across organizational and functional boundaries while accountability remains clear. 

 S.Public creates a place where customers, partners, and experts can explore and discuss these possibilities. The SAP capabilities behind them extend far beyond Berlin. 

 The future of public services will not be determined by how much technology public administrations adopt, but by what they enable for people and society. 

 Andre Bechtold is president of SAP Industries & Experiences and chief revenue officer of Industry AI at SAP.

A hands-on walkthrough of the Google Drive activities in the Google Workspace SDK: searching for folders and files, moving a file into another folder, and renaming it. 
 Introduction 
 This is the sixth post in the series. The fourth post covered the one-time setup for Google Workspace: the OAuth client in Google Cloud Console, the External Authentication in Control Tower, and registering it on the Desktop Agent. The fifth used that setup to go through the Gmail activities. This post uses the same foundation for Google Drive. 
 Drive is a natural companion to Gmail. Attachments, invoices and reports often end up in Drive folders, and an automation needs to find them, organise them and sometimes rename them. We build one task automation that does exactly that, and along the way look at how the query field works, since it's what makes the search activities flexible. 
 Here's what we'll cover: 
 Listing folders and files, with and without a query 
 Finding a folder or file by name 
 Moving a file into a folder and renaming it, using IDs returned by the earlier steps 
 Writing Drive search queries 
 The Google Drive activity group is larger than what we use here. This post covers six of its activities, plus Select Google Authentication and Disconnect (Google). 
 The Drive Activities at a Glance 
 Searching for "drive" in the Tools panel lists the Google Drive activities: Rename File, Move File, Get Folder By Name, Get File By Name, Get File, Get Folder, Download File, Share To Email, Share To Domain, Share With Anyone, Delete File Or Folder and Upload File. The six highlighted in red are the ones used in this post, and they are all visible in the flow on the left. 

 The automation flow with the six Drive activities highlighted, next to the Google Drive activities in the Tools panel. 
 The flow is a straight line with no branches: 
 Step 1: Select Google Authentication. 
 Steps 2 to 5: Get Folder, twice (once without a query, once with one). 
 Steps 6 and 7: Get Folder By Name. 
 Steps 8 to 11: Get File, and Get File By Name. 
 Steps 12 to 15: Move File, then Rename File. 
 Step 16: Disconnect (Google). 
 Almost every activity is followed by a Log Message step that prints the activity's output, so we can see in the test console what Drive returned. All the Drive activities return their results in an output called metaDatas (or a simple true result for move and rename), and the number in front of it in the screenshots is the step that produced it. 
 Before You Start 
 Complete the setup from the fourth post . In Google Cloud Console, the Google Drive API must be enabled and the Drive scope added under Data Access. 
 In Control Tower, the External Authentication you select must include the Drive scope. The authentication in the fourth post only selected Gmail, so add Drive, then register the authentication on the Desktop Agent again so Google's consent screen asks for Drive access too. 
 The Drive scope gives access to all files in the Drive of the account you sign in with, so use a test account for experiments like this one. 
 For the test I created a Drive folder named SAP BPA TEST holding a few invoice PDFs, and, inside it, an empty folder named BPA Moved File that will receive the moved file. This is the Drive before the automation runs: 

 The SAP BPA TEST folder before the run: the empty BPA Moved File folder and three PDFs. 
 Part 1: Get Folder 
 Get Folder (Google Drive) searches for folders. It has three optional inputs: driveId (to target a specific drive), query, and timeout. The output, metaDatas, is the list of folders found. 
 Get Folder without a query. I left all inputs empty. In my test, this returned every folder in my Drive. 

 Get Folder (Google Drive) with no query. 
 Get Folder Log. A Log Message step takes metaDatas from step 2 as its message. I show this log step only once, because every other log step in the flow works the same way. The full list of folders it prints is long, so I'm not including that output. 

 Log Message printing the metaDatas output of step 2. 
 Get Folder with a query. The second Get Folder step narrows the search with this query: mimeType = 'application/vnd.google-apps.folder' and name contains 'SAP'. It returns folders whose names contain a word starting with SAP. 

 Get Folder (Google Drive) - 2 with a query. 
 The log of this step (step 5) shows what came back: the SAP BPA TEST folder, with its ID, creation time and modification time. The IDs are hidden in the screenshot. 

 Log output of step 5: the matching folder. 
 Writing Drive Queries 
 The query field follows Google's Drive search query syntax, the same one the Drive API uses. A query has three parts: a term to search on, an operator, and a value, and parts can be combined with and, or, and not. Google's search query reference lists all valid terms and operators. These are the ones I find most useful: 
 name contains 'SAP' matches items whose name has a word beginning with SAP. 
 name = 'BPA_Demo_Invoice.pdf' matches an exact name. 
 mimeType = 'application/vnd.google-apps.folder' matches folders only. For PDFs, use mimeType = 'application/pdf'. 
 mimeType = 'application/pdf' and name contains 'Invoice' combines two conditions. 
 'FOLDER_ID' in parents and trashed = false lists items directly inside a folder, excluding items in the Trash. Replace FOLDER_ID with the folder's ID. 
 modifiedTime > '2026-10-01T00:00:00' matches items modified after a date (RFC 3339 format). 
 fullText contains 'invoice' searches names, descriptions and the indexed content of files. 
 A few rules worth knowing: 
 Values go in single quotes. A single quote inside a value must be escaped with a backslash, for example name contains 'Bob\'s'. 
 name contains only matches the beginning of words. Google's example: for an item named HelloWorld, name contains 'Hello' finds it, but name contains 'World' does not. 
 To leave out items in the Trash, add trashed = false. 
 In this post I tested the name and mimeType terms. The other terms are documented by Google for the Drive API, but I'd recommend trying them in a test folder first. 
 Part 2: Get Folder By Name 
 When you only know a folder's name, Get Folder By Name (Google Drive) is simpler than writing a query. Its required input is name , which I set to BPA Moved File. The name doesn't have to be complete; in my tests a partial name matched as well. 

 Get Folder By Name (Google Drive) with the folder name. 
 The log of step 7 shows one folder returned: BPA Moved File. Its ID is what the Move File step uses later. 

 Log output of step 7: the BPA Moved File folder. 
 Part 3: Get File and Get File By Name 
 Files have their own pair of activities. Get File (Google Drive) has the same inputs as Get Folder (driveId, query, timeout) and returns files. With no query it returns files from the whole Drive, so I don't show its log, which is a long list. 

 Get File (Google Drive) with no query. 
 Get File By Name (Google Drive) takes a required fileName . I used BPA_Demo, a partial name, so it matches every file whose name starts that way. 

 Get File By Name (Google Drive) with a partial file name. 
 Because the name was partial, the log of step 11 lists several files: BPA_Demo_Invoice.pdf, BPA_Demo_Invoice_Approval_01.pdf and BPA_Demo_Invoice_AutoApproval_02.pdf. In this run, the first item in the list was BPA_Demo_Invoice.pdf, which is the file I want to move. 

 Log output of step 11: the files matching the partial name. 
 Part 4: Move File 
 Move File (Google Drive) needs two IDs, both taken from earlier steps: 
 fileId: metaDatas[0].id from step 10, the first file returned by Get File By Name. 
 destinationFolderId: metaDatas[0].id from step 6, the folder returned by Get Folder By Name. 
 The two steps that provide the IDs are marked in red in the flow. The output result is true when the move succeeded. 

 Move File (Google Drive), with its two IDs coming from steps 10 and 6. 
 Part 5: Rename File 
 Rename File (Google Drive) takes fileId and newName . A move doesn't change a file's ID, so I reuse metaDatas[0].id from step 10 and rename the file to Moved_File.pdf. Include the extension in the new name, because the name you enter is the whole name. 

 Rename File (Google Drive), reusing the file ID from step 10. 
 The logs for steps 13 and 15 simply print the true result of Move File and Rename File: 

 Move File Log and Rename File Log, both printing true. 
 Finishing Up: Disconnect (Google) 
 The last step, Disconnect (Google) , closes the connection to Google when the work is done. 
 Running It 
 I ran the automation from the designer. The test console prints the results of each log step. Some entries are hidden, because they contain names and IDs from my Drive. The final two entries are the true results of Move File and Rename File. The warning at the end only says the testing session has stopped. 

 The test console, with IDs and some names hidden. 
 In Drive, BPA_Demo_Invoice.pdf is no longer in the SAP BPA TEST folder: 

 The SAP BPA TEST folder after the run. 
 Inside the BPA Moved File folder, the file is now called Moved_File.pdf: 

 The BPA Moved File folder after the run, holding the renamed file. 
 Things to Keep in Mind 
 Check which item you take from the list. Partial names can match several items, and the steps above use metaDatas[0], the first one. Here the first match was the file I wanted, but I wouldn't rely on the order. Use a more specific name or query, or look through metaDatas for the item you need. 
 Guard against empty results. If a search finds nothing, a later step that reads metaDatas[0] has nothing to read. Add a condition after each search, as in the Gmail posts. 
 Add error handling. These activities can throw a GoogleDriveError. I left out Try / Catch to keep the flow readable, but you should wrap the Drive steps in one in a real automation. 
 Avoid logging full lists. Get Folder and Get File without a query return everything they can find, which makes long logs in a large Drive. Use a query to narrow results. 
 Treat logs as sensitive. They include file and folder IDs, and for files, download links. Hide them in screenshots you share. 
 Test-mode token expiry. As mentioned in the fourth post, an External app in Testing status has a limited refresh token lifetime. If authorization fails after about a week, register the authentication on the Desktop Agent again. 
 Wrapping Up 
 With a handful of activities, a BPA automation can search a Drive by name or by query, organise files into folders and rename them, all driven by the IDs that earlier steps return. The same Google setup from the fourth post serves both Gmail and Drive. The other Drive activities in the Tools panel (Download, Share, Delete and Upload) aren't covered in this post.

title: Building a Knowledge Home for SAP GTS Preference Management
author: AttilaPayer
text:
When our team started looking at how we handle knowledge transfer, one thing became clear: the expertise existed, it just lived in people's heads. 
 SAP GTS Preference Management is a specialist topic. It sits at the intersection of global trade compliance and supply chain operations, and mastering it takes time, experience, and access to the right guidance. Onboarding a new colleague used to mean leaning heavily on whoever happened to be available. Solving a tricky customer case meant digging through scattered resources or relying on tribal knowledge. We knew we could do better. 
 The Project 
 Over the past months, our team took on an ambitious documentation initiative: building a comprehensive, structured wiki dedicated entirely to SAP GTS Preference Management. Around 30 pages, covering concepts, processes, configuration, and common pitfalls, now form a living knowledge base that anyone on the team or any interested customer can access. 
 The goals were straightforward: 
 Support new colleagues with a reliable starting point, so they can get up to speed faster. 
 Raise our collective knowledge level by making expert insight visible and searchable. 
 Create a centralized resource that is accessible not just internally, but also to our customers who want to understand the subject more deeply. 

 Why It Matters 
 Preference Management in SAP GTS is not a topic with a lot of readily available, consolidated documentation in the community. Customers navigating supplier declarations or preferential origin calculations often find themselves in need of additional information. Our goal was to change that, at least within our sphere of influence. 
 What made this project genuinely exciting was the participant's enthusiasm. This was not a top-down mandate. People contributed because they saw the value, because they wanted to leave things better than they found them, and because sharing knowledge is part of how this community grows. 
 Early Results 
 The real test of any knowledge base is whether people actually use it. We did not have to wait long for an answer. 
 We have already been able to reference the wiki directly when working through customer cases. Having a well-structured, reliable resource to consult and to share with customers has already made a tangible difference in how we work. That is the metric we care about most. 
 An Invitation 
 If you work with SAP GTS Preference Management, whether as a customer, a consultant, or a fellow support engineer, we hope this resource is useful to you. And if you have knowledge to contribute, perspectives to add, or feedback on what would make it even better, we would love to hear from you. 
 Preference Management | SAP Help Portal 
 Knowledge grows when it is shared. This is our contribution to that effort.

title: FSA Integration - How to Enable Parallel Processing in SAP Data Replication Framework (DRF)
author: _Abhinav_Singh
text:
Introduction 
 Replicating large amount of master data from SAP S/4HANA to SAP Field Service and Asset Management (FSA) can take a very long time. If the system sends the data one by one, it creates a traffic jam that slows down your business. 
 The Data Replication Framework (DRF) Parallel Processing feature fixes this problem. Instead of sending everything in a single line, it chops the data into smaller chunks and sends them all at the exact same time. In this blog, I will explain how this process works using Equipment Replication as our example, and show you how to turn it on in your system. 
 DRF configuration 
 1.Business system and replication model: In transaction DRFIMG , maintain the business system under Define Technical Settings for Business Systems . Then create the replication model under Define Replication Model. 

 2. Outbound implementation: Assign the equipment outbound implementation (<your outbound implementation>) and the target business system to the replication model 

 3.Parameter values: On the outbound implementation assignment, maintain below parameter with Values. 

 Parameter 
 Purpose 

 TASK_SIZE_PROCMSG 
 Number of messages handled by one parallel task 

 PACK_SIZE_BULK 
 Number of objects packed into one bulk message call 

 PARALLEL_PROCESS_NEW 
 Enable Parallel processing 

 4.Run with parallel processing: In DRFOUT , select the replication model and the parallel processing checkbox, then execute or schedule it as a background job. 

 How DRF Parallel processes work with 100K equipment: 
 The settings used in this example are: 

 Item 
 Value 
 Result 

 Total messages 
 1,00,000 
 Equipment to process 

 TASK_SIZE_PROCMSG 
 1000 
 ⌈100,000 / 1000⌉ = 100 parallel tasks 

 PACK_SIZE_BULK 
 100 
 10 Send_message calls per task, 1,000 in total 

 Free work processes 
 10 
 Only 10 tasks run at the same time 

 Rounds 
 ⌈100 / 10⌉ 
 10 rounds 
 Only the execution changes. The 100 tasks are pipelined across the 10 work processes: 
 Round 1: Tasks 1– 10 run in parallel (Equipment 1 – 10,000) 
 Round 2: Tasks 11– 20 run in parallel (Equipment 10,001 – 20,000) 
 …… 
 ……. 
 ……. 
 Round 10: Tasks 91–100 run in parallel (Equipment 90,001 – 100,000) 
 Each work processes about 10 tasks one after another: 
 WP-1: [Task 1] → [Task 11] → [Task 21] → ... → [Task 91] 
 WP-2: [Task 2] → [Task 12] → [Task 22] → ... → [Task 92] 
 ... 
 WP-10: [Task 10] → [Task 20] → [Task 30] → ... → [Task 100] 
 Conclusion: 
 With 100,000 equipment, a task size of 1000, and a bulk size of 100, DRF creates 100 tasks that send 10 bulk calls each. With only 10 free work processes, the tasks run in 10 rounds instead of a single parallel round. The work processes limit the elapsed time, not the task and bulk settings. If you can’t get more work processes, a larger task size reduces the task count but doesn’t speed up the run once all 10 work processes are busy. Fewer, larger tasks can even leave work processes idle at the end of the run. Size the task so that the number of tasks is a multiple of the free work processes and tune the bulk size against the target system’s limits. 
 Please share your experiences in the comments.

title: SAP Sustainability Footprint Management - GHG Emissions Calculation based on SAP TM Data
author: thomsensoeren
text:
Transport emissions are often calculated separately from the systems used to plan and execute logistics. As a result, sustainability teams may rely on averages or manually reconstructed transport chains, while logistics teams work with detailed information about freight units, stops, routes, legs, products, quantities, and modes of transport. 
 Bringing these perspectives together can make transport-footprint results more representative and more useful for operational decisions. SAP Sustainability Footprint Management can use detailed transport activity data from SAP Transportation Management or other transportation management systems to calculate and analyze emissions across complex transport chains.

title: SAP Green Ledger: Q3-26 Release Updates and Highlights
author: Julia1501
text:
Welcome to the Q3 2026 edition of our SAP Green Ledger Quarterly Release Highlights! This blog summarizes the most important innovations and enhancements delivered for during Q3 2026. 
 This quarter brought several new capabilities and enhancements to SAP Green Ledger, including faster master data imports with delta loads, new APIs for integrating carbon data from external sources, carbon allocations from energy flows, and more flexible GHG analysis. Further enhancements improve CBAM liability management and usability. 
 Read on to learn more about the key innovations introduced throughout Q3 2026: 
 Faster Master Data Imports with Delta Loads 
 API-Based Carbon Data Imports 
 Enhanced Carbon Data Import Details 
 Carbon Allocations from Energy Flows 
 WBS Elements for Manual Journal Entries 
 Enhanced Carbon Liability Management 
 More Flexible GHG Analysis in the Carbon Data Dashboard 
 Enhanced Carbon and Financial Analysis in the Analytical Dashboard 
 Further Updates and Enhancements 

 Faster Master Data Imports with Delta Loads 
 The Manage Master Data Imports app now supports delta loads in addition to full loads when importing master data from a connected SAP S/4HANA system, enabling faster and more efficient master data imports. Instead of importing the complete master data scope with every import, a delta load imports only newly created and changed master data objects since the previous full or delta load. This reduces the amount of data that needs to be processed and can significantly shorten the time required for the import. 
 Delta Load Option for Master Data Import from Connected SAP S/4HANA System 
 Delta loads are currently supported for account, account hierarchy, product, and project master data in both SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition and SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition. For cost center master data, delta loads are currently supported for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. Other master data objects continue to be imported in full, even when the import is started as a delta load. The first master data import is always performed as a full load. A full load may also be required for subsequent imports, for example when changes are made to the relevant business system. 
 For more information, see SAP Help: Import Master Data . 

 API-Based Carbon Data Imports 
 SAP Green Ledger now provides three APIs for importing and processing carbon data from external sources. In addition to importing emission data from external sources via CSV files, the new APIs now provide a defined interface for integrating this data into SAP Green Ledger. The APIs support the different steps of the carbon data import process, from importing carbon data to releasing an import and monitoring its processing status. 
 The Carbon Data Import API allows you to import carbon data and create the data for the corresponding carbon collections. The Carbon Data Import Release API can then be used to release an import and trigger the creation of the corresponding carbon collections and journal entries. To monitor the process, the Carbon Data Import Status API provides information about the status of an import and the processing results of the corresponding carbon collections. 
 For more information, see the API Guide for SAP Green Ledger . 

 Enhanced Carbon Data Import Details 
 Once carbon data has been imported into SAP Green Ledger, it is important to understand how the data has been processed and what resulted from the import. 
 The Manage Carbon Data Imports app now provides more detailed information about your carbon data imports. You can review the imported data as well as the carbon collections and journal entries created from an import and navigate between them. This provides greater transparency into the results of a carbon data import and makes it easier to trace the imported data through to the resulting carbon collections and journal entries. The enhanced overview and navigation are available for new carbon data imports; existing imports remain unchanged. 
 For more information, see SAP Help: Import Material Movements . 

 Carbon Allocations from Energy Flows 
 Energy flow models in represent how energy and the associated emissions are distributed across different elements of an organization. SAP Green Ledger now brings this information into carbon accounting to reflect the corresponding carbon allocations between cost centers. To support this, the import of modeled energy flows from SAP Sustainability Footprint Management has been extended. In addition to carbon emissions for energy sources, emissions for other nodes in the energy flow, such as facilities, meters, resources, and process infrastructures, are now also imported. 
 Using the Manage Carbon Data Imports app, you can import and release energy flows from a connected SAP Sustainability Footprint Management system. The imported data includes the cost center assignments of the individual nodes, which are carried into the corresponding carbon collections. When these carbon collections are posted to the journal, SAP Green Ledger creates the corresponding cost center-to-cost center allocations based on the modeled energy flow. The resulting journal entries include the respective cost centers and partner cost centers. 
 The carbon collections and resulting journal entries can be reviewed in the Manage Carbon Collections and Manage Journal Entries apps. 
 For more information, see SAP Help: Import Energy Flows . 

 WBS Elements for Manual Journal Entries 
 Carbon adjustments and corrections can now also be assigned to specific WBS elements when journal entries are created manually. The Manage Journal Entries app now supports WBS elements and partner WBS elements for manual journal entries. 
 When creating a manual journal entry, you can now assign a WBS element to a line item for eligible accounts. Cost center and WBS element are mutually exclusive and cannot be maintained for the same line item. When a WBS element is selected, the corresponding profit center and segment are automatically derived. 
 The WBS element value help displays WBS elements based on the relevant project and profit center context. The system also checks whether the selected WBS element is available for posting and informs you if any posting restrictions apply. 
 For more information, see SAP Help: Create Journal Entries . 

 Enhanced Carbon Liability Management 
 With the EU CBAM definitive regime in effect since January 2026, imports of certain goods into the European Union can result in carbon liabilities that need to be recognized and valued. SAP Green Ledger supports this process by accounting for the embedded emissions and the resulting carbon liabilities and by determining their fair value based on the corresponding certificate requirements and Emissions Trading System (ETS) prices. In Q3 2026, new enhancements provide further support for the valuation and review of these liabilities. 
 Official EU ETS Prices 
 The Configure Carbon Certificate Data app now displays the official quarterly ETS prices published by the European Union. These prices are automatically imported into SAP Green Ledger and used for the fair value calculation of carbon liabilities associated with imports subject to EU CBAM. You can view the official quarterly prices together with your maintained ETS prices in the Emissions Trading System Prices tab. 
 Official EU ETS Prices Imported for Quarter 1 and 2 
 A color indicator shows whether ETS prices are available for the current year and quarter: green indicates that prices are maintained for all calendar weeks, while blue indicates that the automatically imported official quarterly EU ETS prices are used. 
 For more information, see SAP Help: View and Maintain Emissions Trading System Prices . 
 Product Information in Carbon Liabilities 
 The Manage Carbon Liabilities app now displays the Product selected for carbon collections that require carbon certificates, providing additional context when reviewing carbon liabilities. 
 For more information, see SAP Help: View Carbon Liabilities and Create a Carbon Collection . 

 More Flexible GHG Analysis in the Carbon Data Dashboard 
 The Carbon Data Dashboard has been enhanced with new options for analyzing GHG emissions. 
 The timing of GHG emission recognition can differ depending on whether emissions are considered when carbon data is posted or when the underlying resources are actually consumed. You can now choose between the accrual and non-accrual accounting method, which determines how GHG emissions are calculated and displayed in the dashboard. 
 With the non-accrual method, GHG emissions are recognized when carbon-relevant data is posted to the GHG Liabilities Collection account . The resulting GHG emissions therefore represent the emissions recorded at the time of the carbon data posting, regardless of subsequent activities related to the underlying resources. 
 With the accrual method, emissions are distinguished based on whether the underlying resources have already been consumed. Emissions related to consumed resources are recognized as realized GHG emissions in profit and loss accounts, while emissions related to resources that have not yet been consumed remain as accrued emissions in balance sheet accounts. As the resources are consumed, the corresponding emissions move from the balance sheet to profit and loss. This allows the dashboard to reflect GHG emissions in line with actual resource consumption. 
 Selection of Accrued and Non-Accrued GHG Emissions Overview 
 The Carbon Data Dashboard also introduces an enhancement to the WBS Element filter. The filter is now organized by project, with a project node at the top of the hierarchy grouping the corresponding WBS elements. This provides clearer context and makes it easier to locate and select WBS elements within their associated projects. 
 Enhanced WBS Element Filter Organized by Project 
 For more information, see SAP Help: Analyze Carbon Data and Accounting Method . 

 Enhanced Carbon and Financial Analysis in the Analytical Dashboard 
 The SAP Green Ledger Analytical Dashboard has also been updated for Q3 2026 with enhancements to filtering and data visualization. The updates make it easier to analyze carbon data in the context of projects and WBS elements and further improve the presentation and interpretation of GHG and financial data. 
 For a detailed overview of the latest SAP Green Ledger Analytical Dashboard enhancements, see the dedicated SAP Community blog post and the SAP Help Portal topic Analyze Carbon Data Alongside Financial Data . 

 Further Updates and Enhancements 
 Several smaller enhancements further improve the usability of SAP Green Ledger. 
 Line Item Totals and Subtotals 
 The Line Items table in the Manage Journal Entries app now displays debit and credit totals and subtotals. When line items are grouped by an attribute, you can view the corresponding subtotals for each group, making it easier to analyze and review carbon-related postings. 
 Filtering by Empty Dimension Values 
 The Manage Journal Entries , Display Line Items , and Display Account Balances apps now allow you to filter for empty or unassigned values across supported dimensions, including, for example, WBS element, cost center, product, and supplier. You can display only postings where a particular dimension has not been assigned, or exclude these postings from the results. This makes it easier to review postings based on whether specific dimension information is available. 
 Journal Entry IDs Without Leading Zeros 
 Journal entry IDs are now displayed without leading zeros across SAP Green Ledger, making them easier to read, search, and sort. This applies wherever journal entry IDs are displayed. 
 Documentation Feedback on SAP Help Portal 
 You can now provide feedback directly on the Admin Guide, Integration Guide, API Guide, and Introduction for SAP Green Ledger on SAP Help Portal. This makes it easier to share feedback on

title: Precautions for locking DDIC in all clients and TMSADM in non-000 clients in S/4HANA 2020
author: SAPSupport
text:
For security reasons, we need to lock the standard user DDIC in all clients of our SAP S/4HANA system. We also need to lock the standard user TMSADM in all clients except client 000. 
 Before we perform these changes, please advise: 
 What should be checked or adjusted before and after locking DDIC in all clients to avoid system errors or background job failures? 
 What should be checked or adjusted before and after locking TMSADM in all clients except client 000 to avoid transport or system errors?

title: AI-powered Proactive Weather Monitoring to safeguard SAP CX Utilities' Customers
author: alinemarchetti
text:
The SAP Mission Control Center (MCC), in partnership with SAP’s Technical Support team, is launching a proactive weather-monitoring pilot program designed to protect our most critical SAP Customer Experience (CX) Utilities customers during severe weather events. Rather than waiting for tickets to surface, we proactively engage by performing advance critical health checks before a weather event makes landfall to help ensure 100% uptime for utility providers whose SAP-powered call centers are essential to emergency response operations. 
 This pilot initially focuses on 5 nominated SAP Cloud for Customer (C4C) and SAP Service Cloud customers in geographically high-risk regions across North America, with the goal of providing advance warning 3-5 days before the event. 
 T h e challenge: Why is severe weather critical for utilities CX? 
 Utility providers are the first responders during weather-driven infrastructure failures. During a major storm event, their SAP CX platforms, particularly SAP Cloud for Customer and SAP Service Cloud, serve as the operational backbone for coordinating field crews, managing large-scale outages, and communicating with hundreds of thousands of affected customers. 
 Key risk factors 
 Sudden surges in call volume can overwhelm the call center running on SAP. 
 Unresolved platform incidents during emergencies can directly endanger the public. 
 Traditional reactive support models may be insufficient for life-safety scenarios, underscoring the need for predictive and preventive approaches. 
 Call center continuity is mission-critical: disruptions can impede emergency coordination. 
 Our approach: proactive engagement over reactive response 
 The fundamental shift in this program is a shift in posture. We move from incident-driven response to forecasted-risk-driven mobilization: proactively identifying threats and deploying resources before a customer needs to raise a Priority 1 (P1) incident. 

 Reactive (Old Model) 
 Proactive (Our Approach) 

 Wait for the customer to raise a P1 Monitor weather threats 3–5 days in advance 

 Mobilize SAP MCC resources after the event 
 Activate Critical Period Coverage (CPC) proactively prior to landfall 
 How it works: monitor, assess, and activate our Critical Period Coverage portfolio offering 
 The program follows a 3-phase period coverage activation. 
 Step 1: Monitor 
 AI tools continuously scan authoritative weather data feeds for the geographic regions associated with each pilot customer. Monitoring runs daily and continuously throughout the pilot period. 
 Step 2: Assess 
 When a potential threat is identified, the system determines the geographic impact area, event duration, severity, and proximity to each customer’s service territory. This produces a per-customer risk score . 
 Step 3: Activate the SAP MCC Critical Period Coverage o ffering 
 If the risk score exceeds the activation threshold, the critical period coverage is triggered. The SAP MCC assigns a Critical Customer Manager to the account who acts as the single point of contact, notifies the account team and, if necessary, the customer, and begins active monitoring of system utilization and incident queues for the duration of the event. 
 Collaboration across LoBs 
 The SAP MCC aligns with experts from the SAP Technical Support organization and the CX Operations teams to determine whether the system is adequately sized and whether scale-up or sizing changes are required. In addition, the SAP MCC will collaborate with Technical Support to review the customer’s configuration and run proactive health checks in advance of the event to proactively mitigate risk and help maintain 100% uptime during the storm. 
 Post-event, the SAP MCC will document the engagement, capture lessons learned, and channel findings back into the program to improve risk scoring and response thresholds. 
 A I -powered weather intelligence - Power e d by AI / Joule 
 The 3-to-5-day warning window is made possible by an AI-assisted monitoring layer that continuously ingests real-time and forecast weather data and correlates it with the precise geographic footprint of each pilot customer’s service territory. 
 How the AI layer works: 
 Continuous Weather Monitoring 
 AI tools (powered by Claude/Joule Studio) continuously ingest real-time and forecast weather data feeds from authoritative sources, with algorithms that identify events matching defined severity and geographic thresholds. 
 Daily alerts are automatically issued to prevent missed events, while 
 notifications are triggered 3-5 days before landfall and delivered directly via email and mobile. 
 Customer Risk Assessment & Scoring 
 Customer service regions are mapped to storm tracks to determine the likelihood of impact. 
 Duration, intensity, and affected population density are factored into a composite risk model. Joule evaluates and provides a risk percentage for threats to critical infrastructure based on the weather event/region and produces a ranked per- customer risk score that defines the critical p eriod c overage activation level. 
 Communications Generation 
 Internal and external communications are automatically generated based on the ongoing weather event and reported customer issues, ensuring timely and consistent messaging throughout the event lifecycle. 
 Customer Incident Dashboard 
 A real-time customer incident dashboard is created and actively monitored throughout the duration of the critical period coverage . 
 This is powered by SAP Joule providing a centralized view of customer impact, open incidents, and status tracking. 
 Pi l ot s c o pe : 5 fo c us C X ut i l ities customers 
 The initial pilot focuses on 5 SAP Customer Experience customers across Florida, California, Arkansas, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Texas and Virginia. 
 These customers were nominated based on weather exposure, geographic risk profile and business criticality. The primary focus is on call center deployments which is directly linked to emergency response capability. 
 W ha t to expect 
 When the SAP MCC identifies a threat 
 SAP MCC will proactively reach out to the SAP Customer Success Manager 3–5 days before a forecast event. 
 The front office teams will receive event details: affected region, severity, expected duration, and the customer risk score. 
 A named SAP MCC resource will be introduced as the dedicated contact for the critical period coverage (customer-facing if appropriate). 
 During the event 
 The SAP MCC will communicate directly with the customer contact to streamline the response. 
 SAP Technical Support will run health checks to help ensure 100% system uptime during the event. 
 The account team will be copied on all critical communications and escalation notifications. 
 Af ter t h e event 
 The SAP Mission Control Center will debrief with the front office team and document the engagement. Feedback is used to improve the risk scoring model for future events.
